raw.text: At the pre-target stage, the petitioner alleged that Hakim Rai, the original tenant of the ground-floor shop at property no.95, Main Bazar, Najafgarh, Delhi, had sublet it to his son-in-law Raj Kumar and completely divested himself of the suit property.
In his pre-target defence, Hakim Rai stated that he was elderly, ailing, and losing his eyesight, and that he had requested Raj Kumar to assist with his business during the latter part of 1983.

The pre-target case narrative reports a partnership deed dated 20.11.1983, Ex.AW-3/13, between Hakim Rai and Raj Kumar, providing that their partnership business would operate from the suit premises. The reported instrument's authenticity remains disputed.
At the pre-target stage, the landlord contended that Ex.AW-3/13 was fake and forged, created as a sham defence to the eviction petition under Section 14(1)(b).

RW-1 Sumitra Devi, Hakim Rai's widow, testified that her husband initially operated the shop, she also participated in its business, and Raj Kumar was her husband's business partner. She denied that Hakim Rai had ceased possessing or conducting business after Raj Kumar's induction. She did not know whether Hakim Rai had deposited rent and testified that he became blind approximately one and a half years before his death.

The pre-target case narrative states that Hakim Rai and Raj Kumar resided at the same premises and Raj Kumar had obtained a ration card at that address. It also identifies execution of their partnership deed in November 1983. The residential address is not independently established as identical to the demised shop.
PW-3, the landlord's attorney, admitted that Hakim Rai was elderly, had very poor eyesight, and could not walk properly.

raw.description: The disputed arrangement concerns the ground-floor shop at property no.95, Main Bazar, Najafgarh, Delhi, originally let to Hakim Rai. Raj Kumar, Hakim Rai's son-in-law, became involved in the shop business, which the defence associated with assistance requested in late 1983 and the reported partnership deed dated 20.11.1983. The landlord characterizes the same involvement as subletting accompanied by complete divestment, and challenges the partnership deed's authenticity. The actual contractual relationship, control, and legal possession remain contested. Shared residence is contextual and does not independently establish another disposition of the shop.

LAW:S02:DRC14:1b.text:
Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any other law or contract, no order or decree for the recovery of possession of any premises shall be made by any court or Controller in favour of the landlord against a tenant:Provided that the Controller may, on an application made to him in the prescribed manner, make an order for the recovery of possession of the premises on one or more of the following grounds only, namely: -
cite11†(b) that the tenant has, on or after the 9th day of June, 1952, sub-let, assigned or otherwise parted with the possession of the whole or any part of the premises without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord;

IK-190902:L107.text: 30. So long as the lessee retains the legal possession of the whole of the premises he does not commit a breach of law against parting with the possession by allowing other people to use the same. A tenant cannot be said to part with the possession of any part of the premises unless his agreement with the license wholly ousts him from the legal possession of that part. If there is anything in the nature of a right to concurrent user there is no parting with possession: See Stenina v.

IK-190902:L108.text: Abrahama, (1931) f Ch D 470 and G. D. Chaudhary v. Anand Sarup. 1966 Delhi Lt 28.

IK-190902:L109.text: 31. Clause (b) of the proviso to cite8†Section 14(1) uses three expressions namely 'sublet', 'assign' and 'otherwise parted with the possession of the whole or any part of the premises without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord'. These three expressions deal with different concepts and apply to different circumstances.

IK-190902:L110.text: In subletting there exists the relationship of landlord and tenant as between the tenant and his sub-tenant and all the incidents of letting or tenancy have to be found, namely the transfer of an interest in the estate payment of rent, and the right to possession as against the tenant in respect of the Premises sublet. In assignment the tenant has to divest himself of all the rights that he has as a tenant.

IK-190902:L111.text: The expression "parted with possession" undoubtedly postulates parting with possession session means giving possession to persons other than those to whom possession has been given by lease and "parting with possession" must have been by the tenant.

IK-190902:L112.text: The mere user by other persons is no parting with Possession so long as the tenant retains the legal possession himself or in other words there must be vesting of possession by the tenant in another person by divesting himself not only of physical possession but also of the right to possession. The divestment or abandonment of the right to possession is necessary in order to invoke the clause of parting with possession: See cite11†Hazari Lal v. Gian Ram . 1972 Ren Cr 74 (Delhi).
